The join constraint is a finding in itself:

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Multi-input derived nodes here join on **exact timestamp equality**, so a 30 Hz CAN signal and a 99 Hz IMU signal can never be combined into one node — they share literally zero timestamps. - The way around it is to derive the *same physical quantity separately on each clock* — lateral acceleration from GNSS pose, and from the IMU — then compare them. That's a stronger validation anyway, because the two paths share no sensor.

The sideslip result is the cleanest finding in the whole dataset — let me explain before marking events:

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- During the straight cruise (t≈90–190 s, steering ±0.1°, speed ~20 m/s) sideslip sits at a rock-steady **-1.30° to -1.45°**, with under 0.3° of spread per 2 s window. On a straight road at constant speed, true sideslip *must* be ≈0. So this is a **constant heading bias**: the reported yaw under-reads the actual direction of travel by ~1.35°.
- The ±5–8° swings during turns are **my method's artifact, not the vehicle's**: course-over-ground from a 0.25 s chord lags instantaneous heading by about ω·Δt/2 — for ω=0.7 rad/s that is exactly 5.0°. This is why the straight-line segment is the only place the bias can be read honestly, and why it's trustworthy there (ω≈0 ⇒ artifact≈0).

local spd = series("/nissan/vehicle_speed/data")
local acc = series("accel_long_mps2/value")
local lat = series("gps_lat_accel_mps2/value")

-- Merge contiguous hits into ONE region per stretch, then drop stretches
-- too short to be a real manoeuvre (rejects single-sample excursions).
local function regions(s, pred, minDur, mergeGap, label, desc)
  if s == nil then
    return 0
  end
  local segs = {}
  local start, last = nil, nil
  for i = 0, s:size() - 1 do
    local p = s:at(i)
    if p ~= nil then
      if pred(p.v) then
        if start == nil then
          start = p.t
        end
        last = p.t
      elseif start ~= nil then
        segs[#segs + 1] = { start, last }
        start = nil
      end
    end
  end
  if start ~= nil then
    segs[#segs + 1] = { start, last }
  end

  local merged = {}
  for _, sg in ipairs(segs) do
    local m = merged[#merged]
    if m ~= nil and (sg[1] - m[2]) < mergeGap * NS then
      m[2] = sg[2]
    else
      merged[#merged + 1] = { sg[1], sg[2] }
    end
  end

  local n = 0
  for _, sg in ipairs(merged) do
    local dur = (sg[2] - sg[1]) / NS
    if dur >= minDur then
      startMarker(sg[1])
      closeMarker(sg[2], { label = label, description = desc .. string.format(" (%.1f s)", dur) })
      n = n + 1
    end
  end
  return n
end

All 12 artifacts are in place and verified. Here's what the data says.

## The drive

231.5 s, **2.66 km**, mean 11.5 m/s (41 km/h), peak **20.97 m/s (75.5 km/h)**. The log tells a clean story:

| Phase | Time | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Standstill | 0–3 s | v≈0, steering parked at +1.2 |
| Urban manoeuvring | 3–60 s | 1–7 m/s, large steering (+35.4 / −24.3), several turns |
| Hard stop | 23–29 s | **−3.60 m/s²**, the harshest braking in the log; 6.8 → 0.68 m/s |
| Ramp / on-ramp | 60–90 s | accelerating 6→14 m/s **while** cornering; peak accel +4.8 m/s² at ~81 s |
| Sustained curve | 77–87 s | lateral accel held at 2.1→**5.35 m/s² (0.55 g)** for ~10 s |
| Highway cruise | 90–190 s | steering **±0.1°**, 14→21 m/s, lateral accel <0.2 m/s² — dead straight |
| Slow + manoeuvre | 190–215 s | down to 6 m/s, a 4.7 m/s² corner at ~205 s, back up to 16 m/s |
| Final stop | 215–231 s | −2.6 m/s² to standstill |

The sharpest corner is at **t≈64 s**: −5.03 m/s² at 7.4 m/s ⇒ radius ≈ 11 m, yaw rate 0.68 rad/s — which matches the gyro's log-wide maximum of 0.717 rad/s independently.

## What I created

In **Custom Series** (bottom-left panel, *not* the Datasets tree) — drag onto a plot:

| Series | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `speed_kmh`, `distance_m` | readable speed; cumulative odometry (2664 m) |
| `accel_long_mps2` | windowed dv/dt from CAN speed |
| `gps_speed_mps`, `gps_yaw_rate_rps`, `gps_lat_accel_mps2`, `gps_sideslip_deg`, `gps_curvature_1perm` | full vehicle dynamics from GNSS pose alone |
| `imu_accel_mag_mps2`, `imu_gravity_error_mps2` | accelerometer scale/bias check |
| `imu_yaw_rate_from_quat_rps`, `imu_gyro_mean_rps`, `imu_gyro_minus_quat_rps` | orientation-vs-gyro consistency |
| `imu_dt_ms`, `imu_hdr_dt_ms`, `pose_dt_ms`, `can_dt_ms` | timing health per source |
| `mag_magnitude_uT`, `mag_heading_deg` | magnetometer sanity |

Plus **7 global marker regions** (STOPPED / HARSH BRAKE / HARD ACCEL / CORNERING) on all plots.

For the route itself, use PlotJuggler's XY plot with `position/x` on X and `position/y` on Y — no derived series needed.

## What you should take into consideration

**1. All covariances are exactly zero.** Orientation, angular velocity, linear acceleration — every matrix is unfilled. Any EKF or `robot_localization` node consuming these will either reject them or trust them infinitely. This is the single biggest blocker to using this bag for fusion.

**2. GNSS timestamps are delivery times, not sample times.** `imu_dt_ms` ranges 0.15–107.6 ms on a nominal 10 ms period (σ=10.4 ms), and — decisively — `imu_hdr_dt_ms` shows *the same* distribution (σ=10.41, identical 107.58 ms max). The burstiness is in the `header.stamp` itself, so it is not a recording artifact you can undo. **Never differentiate GNSS/INS data on this bag**; use the gyro directly. This is exactly why my first naive derivative produced a 525 m/s "speed". `pose_dt_ms` is worse (σ=26.3 ms on 50 ms). By contrast **`can_dt_ms` is excellent**: σ=0.216 ms on 33.3 ms. The CAN bus is clean; the GNSS is not.

**3. Nothing shares a clock — not even the two CAN topics.** `vehicle_speed` and `vehicle_steering` have identical rates and identical 6948 sample counts, yet **zero timestamps in common**. Every topic is its own clock island. Any speed×steering or speed×yaw-rate product requires explicit resampling, and cross-source latency is unknown and unbounded.

**4. Constant heading bias of ≈ −1.35°.** Detailed above — steady to within 0.3° across 100 s of straight cruising. Likely dual-antenna baseline misalignment. Correctable by a constant offset, but must be corrected.

**5. The two orientation sources disagree.** `/imu/orientation` and `/current_pose/pose/orientation` come from the same Duro, but their statistics differ by ~1.7° in pitch and ~19° in yaw. Means are a weak statistic under bursty sampling, so I'm flagging this rather than asserting it — **overlay the two yaw fields and compare `header/frame_id`** before trusting either. A frame convention difference (ENU vs map) is the likely cause.

**6. Accelerometer reads 2.8% high.** `imu_accel_mag` averages 10.083 m/s² against 9.81 (`accel/z` mean −9.93). A scale or bias error of +0.27 m/s² — small, but it integrates.

**7. `vehicle_steering` is not in steering-wheel degrees.** Its quantum is exactly 0.0063 units (all values are integer multiples). Reconciling steering against measured yaw rate at three separate corners gives a factor of roughly **1.6–2.0× the road-wheel angle** — so it is neither steering-wheel angle (~16×) nor road-wheel angle (1×). The 35.4° peak, taken as a road-wheel angle, would imply 1.16 rad/s of yaw, and the gyro never exceeds 0.717. **Calibrate this signal before use**; my factor is approximate precisely because of finding #3.

**8. The magnetometer is unusable as-is.** Magnitude averages 48.7 µT (correct for Hungary) but swings 23.1–58.4 µT with σ=4.6 — heavy hard/soft-iron disturbance from the vehicle — and it's quantised to 1 µT.

**9. `position/z` is identically 0.** This is a 2D projection; there is no altitude data.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The cross-validation that *does* hold is worth noting: GNSS-derived speed averages 11.538 m/s against CAN's 11.507 — agreement to **0.27%** over 2.66 km, through two sensor chains sharing no hardware. So despite all the timing pathology, wheel-speed scaling and GNSS position are mutually consistent; there's no odometry scale error to correct.
- Note the asymmetry in these findings: bias errors (heading −1.35°, accel +2.8%, steering scale) are *correctable post-hoc*, but the zero covariances and bursty timestamps are *destructive* — information that was never recorded can't be recovered.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## One decision I'd like you to make

The event thresholds in the marker rule are a domain call I shouldn't make unilaterally, and they're the main knob on what the markers actually show. I currently use −2.2 m/s² (brake), +2.5 (accel), 2.5 (lateral), each sustained ≥0.5 s — which yields 7 regions marking only genuinely notable events.

Those are **safety-flavoured** thresholds. If your interest is ride *comfort*, the literature figures are much lower (≈1.5 m/s² longitudinal, ≈1.8 m/s² lateral), which would light up the whole urban phase and the on-ramp curve. If you're screening for *aggressive driving*, you'd go the other way — 0.4 g and up.

Tell me which framing you want (or hand me the four numbers) and I'll re-run the marker set. Worth knowing: the marker set is singular — re-running **replaces** the current 7 regions rather than adding to them, so this is a swap, not an accumulation.
